newsitem.title: USA: Consumer bill offered as part of U.S. bank reforms.
newsitem.headline: Consumer bill offered as part of U.S. bank reforms.

text.p: U.S. House lawmaker John LaFalce introduced a bill Tuesday aimed at protecting bank customers as banks expand into a broader array of services, including securities, underwriting and dealing.
The New York Democrat's legislation, co-sponsored by 17 other Democrats on the House Banking Committee, comes as the panel begins debating sweeping bank reform legislation.
"I support financial modernization legislation because I believe it potentially holds out many benefits for consumers," LaFalce said.
But LaFalce warned that consumers will be dealing with banks that may be part of large-scale diversified financial institutions.
"In this environment, consumers potentially become more vulnerable and the risk of confusion increases," he said.
Consumers will no longer simply be using banks to make deposits or purchase a limited selection of investment products, he said.
"The potential for one-stop shopping and consumer savings is real and substantial," the lawmaker said. "But so is the potential for confusion."
The LaFalce measure would mandate bank regulators to make sure several consumer protection steps are taken at financial institutions.
Banks would be required to make clear to their customers when an offered product is not insured and what other risks may be associated with that product.

Banks would be prohibited from making any misrepresentations about the products they offer to customers. They would also be banned from coercing customers into buying certain products or services as a condition for offering other services, a practice commonly called tying.

Under the consumer protection bill, bank regulators would be required to establish a dispute resolution mechanism similar to the securities arbitration process to allow consumers to voice their concerns on any violations of consumer protection issues.
Under the bill, consumers would have more control keeping information about their financial transactions more private.
The bill came as good news for the Consumers Union, a lobbying group representing customers and other retail consumers.

"Consumers are long overdue these protections," said Michelle Meier of the Consumers Union. She added that the current consumer protection guidelines bank regulators have given the banking communities are not enough.
"The guidelines have no enforcement mechanism," Meier said.
Under the bill, regulators would be mandated to establish these rules within six months of enactment of any bank reforms and they would be required to enforce them, LaFalce said.
He warned that any bank expansion should be coupled with consumer protection.
